summaries.example: Imagine a toy that must always be exactly the same. It could not begin, end, grow, shrink, or move. Parmenides asks us to think about something even more basic: what must be real and what could only seem to change. He also gives an account of the changing world, including the sky, Earth, and living things.
summaries.summary: Parmenides was an early Greek philosopher from Elea who wrote a poem about how to investigate reality. In the poem, a goddess describes paths of inquiry. One path concerns what must be: it cannot begin or end, cannot change, and is complete and unified. Another path concerns what cannot be, which cannot truly be understood. A third path is followed by ordinary people, who mix up being and not-being and rely too heavily on changing appearances. Later in the poem, Parmenides presents a cosmology, or account of the universe, including light and night, the heavens, Earth, the moon, and living things. Scholars disagree about whether he meant to reject the everyday world or explain it from a different point of view. A major interpretation says that Parmenides distinguishes what must be from things that exist but could be different.
key_ideas: Parmenides wrote a difficult poem about reality and knowledge.
The poem describes different ways of thinking about what is and what is not.
He argues that what must be real cannot have started, stopped, changed, or become divided.
The poem also describes the changing world, even though the speaker says ordinary beliefs are not fully trustworthy.
People still disagree about how the poem’s two parts fit together.
summaries.why_it_matters: Parmenides helped begin deep philosophical thinking about reality, change, knowledge, and possibility. He showed that a simple question—what does it mean for something to be?—can lead to large arguments about time, motion, and the world. His ideas influenced later Greek philosophers, who tried to answer his challenges while still explaining the changing world we experience.

important_terms.definition: A very old Greek thinker who wrote a poem about reality, change, and how people can know things.
The study of what is real and what kinds of things exist.
Something that cannot fail to be the way it is.
Something that may be one way now but could have been different or may change later.
A careful path of asking questions to reach understanding.

questions_to_think_about: Can something change and still remain the same thing?
Why might Parmenides distrust what our senses tell us?
Is a changing world less real than something that never changes?
Why might a philosopher include a story about the stars and Earth after discussing unchanging reality?

summaries.example: Consider a scientific law or mathematical object. If it is necessary, it could not fail to be what it is. By contrast, a particular tree exists, grows, and dies, but it need not have existed and could have developed differently. On the modal interpretation of Parmenides, the first part of his poem investigates what must be, while the cosmological part describes things that are real but contingent and changeable. This lets the poem treat both an unchanging principle and the experienced cosmos without simply declaring the latter nonexistent.
summaries.summary: Parmenides of Elea composed a difficult philosophical poem that became central to ancient Greek metaphysics and natural philosophy. Its opening presents a journey to a goddess, who sets out the objects and limits of inquiry. The first route concerns what is and cannot not be: what must be. The goddess argues that this object of understanding cannot have been generated or destroyed, cannot be divided, cannot vary internally, cannot move, and must be complete. A second route concerns what is not and must not be; because it is impossible, it cannot be apprehended or indicated. A third route characterizes mortal thinking, which treats changing things as both being and not being the same and therefore fails to achieve stable understanding. The poem then gives a cosmology based on light and night, covering the heavens, Earth, living things, and human thought. The fragments do not settle every interpretive question. Some readers take the first part to deny the reality of the sensible world; others see it as a higher-order account of the requirements for genuine entities; still others understand the two parts as accounts of one cosmos under different aspects. The modal interpretation emphasizes Parmenides’ distinction between what must be, what must not be, and what is but need not be.
key_ideas: Parmenides’ surviving work is part of a hexameter poem whose title, commonly given as On Nature, may not be original.
The proem presents a symbolic journey to a goddess, who promises instruction about both trustworthy reality and mortal opinions.
The poem distinguishes necessary being, necessary non-being, and a third path involving changing things that are and are not the same in different respects or times.
In the Way of Conviction, what must be is argued to be ungenerated, imperishable, whole, uniform, motionless, and complete.
The later cosmology treats light and night as basic principles and discusses celestial bodies, Earth, reproduction, and thought, although much of it survives only in fragments and later reports.
Interpretations range from strict monism and logical-dialectical readings to meta-principle, aspectual, and modal accounts; the central issue is how the poem’s two major phases relate.
summaries.why_it_matters: Parmenides is important because he made modality—the difference between what must be, what cannot be, and what could be otherwise—central to philosophical inquiry. He also helped establish ontology as a distinct field concerned with being rather than only with particular natural processes. His arguments forced later philosophers to explain how plurality, motion, generation, and destruction are possible. The survival of only fragments makes interpretation difficult, but that difficulty also shows how questions about language, thought, perception, and reality can remain connected across the history of philosophy.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of being, existence, and the basic structure of reality.
The view that reality is fundamentally one; this can mean one thing, one substance, or one basic kind, so the term is not unambiguous.
A way of interpreting Parmenides in which the first part describes what must be and the second describes the contingent, changing cosmos.
A mode of being that cannot fail to be; Parmenides links it with what is stable, complete, and unchanging.
A mode of being that is possible but not required; changing things are treated as having this kind of status.
A philosophical account of the universe, including its principles, origins, and operations.
A claim or description about something considered in one respect or aspect rather than in every respect.
The condition of being able to be otherwise, as opposed to being required or impossible.

questions_to_think_about: Does an argument about what can be thought and said establish a claim about what exists, or does it establish a claim about necessary reality?
If changing things are contingent rather than impossible, can Parmenides consistently discuss them in a cosmology?
What is gained by distinguishing necessary being from contingent being?
Should an interpretation give equal weight to the poem’s metaphysical argument and its cosmology?
How might reliance on sensation produce unstable or ‘wandering’ understanding?

summaries.example: Suppose a class is studying a river. Everyone can observe that its water changes, its shape shifts, and its plants grow. Parmenides might ask a deeper question: are these changing features the kind of reality that can provide completely certain knowledge? He distinguishes them from what must be exactly what it is. A later reader could say that the river is real but contingent, while the unchanging object of the first part of the poem has a different kind of reality.
summaries.summary: Parmenides was an early fifth-century BCE philosopher from Elea in southern Italy. His surviving work comes from a challenging poem, probably written in epic verse. Much of the poem is lost, so later quotations and reports help scholars reconstruct it. The poem begins with a journey to a goddess. She promises to teach Parmenides about trustworthy reality and about the beliefs of mortals. Her instructions describe different ways of inquiry. The first asks about what is and cannot not be—what is necessary. The second concerns what is not and must not be, which cannot be thought or described as an object of knowledge. A third path belongs to mortals, who treat being and not-being as if they could be mixed together and whose thinking wanders because it follows changing appearances. Along the first path, Parmenides argues that What Is has no beginning or end, is whole and uniform, does not move, and is complete. The poem then turns to the Way of Mortals, a cosmology involving light and night, the stars, sun, moon, Earth, reproduction, and thought. This creates the main interpretive problem: why give a detailed account of the changing world after arguing about unchanging reality? Some scholars think the world of experience is dismissed; others think the first part describes the requirements for genuine or fundamental beings; still others see the two parts as different perspectives on a world that includes both permanence and change. The modal interpretation emphasizes that Parmenides distinguishes necessary being from contingent beings, rather than simply denying that changing things exist.
key_ideas: Parmenides’ poem uses a journey and a goddess to introduce lessons about reality and human opinion.
It presents two genuine routes for understanding: what is and cannot not be, and what is not and must not be.
It also describes a third route followed by mortals, who confuse being and not-being while relying on changing appearances.
The unchanging reality in the first part is described as complete, unified, and without beginning or end.
The poem’s second part gives a natural explanation involving light, night, the heavens, Earth, and living things.
Scholars disagree about whether Parmenides rejected the ordinary world, analyzed the conditions for fundamental reality, or described different aspects of one world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Parmenides matters because he made philosophers examine assumptions that often go unnoticed. We usually accept change, plurality, and time as obvious, but he asks what must be true for these ideas to make sense. His poem also connects logic, language, perception, and natural science. Later thinkers developed new physical theories partly in response to questions raised by him. Even when readers reject a strict interpretation of his conclusions, they continue to use his distinctions to think about existence, possibility, certainty, and change.

important_terms.definition: The study of reality: what exists and what the basic features of existence are.
The view that reality is one in some important sense. Philosophers disagree about whether this means one object, one substance, or one basic kind.
A path or method for investigating a question.
Something that has to be the way it is and cannot be otherwise.
Something that exists or is a certain way but could have been different.
An explanation of the universe and its parts, such as the stars, Earth, and living things.
The study of how we know things and how reliable different sources of knowledge are.
An interpretation that treats the poem’s two accounts as descriptions of the same world in different respects.

questions_to_think_about: Why does Parmenides think the path of what cannot be cannot lead to knowledge?
Are changing things unreal, or might they simply be less certain than what does not change?
What could Parmenides gain by writing both a metaphysical argument and a cosmology?
Does calling Parmenides a monist tell us enough about his position?
Can the senses and reason both contribute to understanding, or must one replace the other?
